primary_category.subcategory: A2.4 Information search, retrieval, gathering, and evaluation

evidence.quote: I did register that the item was irregular, non-palletized, heavier than usual—that did cross my mind—but the system's had a good run, so I went with it.
evidence.explanation: The participant evaluates a system-generated output against known cargo characteristics before deciding whether to accept it.

evidence.quote: I looked at the total weight and it was basically in line with the LMCs we'd been getting all week on this route... So I cleared it on that basis.
evidence.explanation: The participant retrieves historical data and compares it against new information to evaluate whether the LMC required further action.

evidence.quote: I pulled up the dispatch log because I wanted a sanity check before signing off, given the tail-heavy reading from the ramp.
evidence.explanation: Explicit act of retrieving and evaluating records (dispatch log) to inform a decision.

evidence.quote: At the time, what did your own calculated index for this flight actually show? ... It was within the normal range on its own, forward of the aft limit with margin.
evidence.explanation: The participant computes and interprets a numerical weight-and-balance index against structural limits.

evidence.quote: roughly 380 kilos of mail plus six late bags... A couple of extra minutes with the trim computer.
evidence.explanation: Reasoning involves quantifying weights and considering a specific numerical index-shift calculation.

evidence.quote: Two in a row felt like enough to say something was going on with how this rotation was trending that day.
evidence.explanation: The participant forms a generalised explanatory model (a rotation-level trend) from discrete prior events, an abstraction beyond the immediate data point.

evidence.quote: so I shifted some of the cargo distribution forward before finalizing, beyond what my own computed index actually called for.
evidence.explanation: The participant devises and applies a non-routine adjustment to cargo distribution as a contingency response to combined evidence, going beyond a purely computed value.

evidence.quote: I issued the ALI to the ramp pretty much as generated so they could start loading, because we were already tight on time.
evidence.explanation: The participant directs ramp activity and coordinates the sequencing of loading operations against a time constraint, and receives operational feedback from ramp personnel.

not_observed_or_insufficient: A1.1 Strength — no evidence of the participant exerting physical force; loading is performed by ramp personnel, not described from the participant's own physical involvement.
A1.2 Dexterity — no evidence of fine manual manipulation by the participant.
A1.3 Navigation — no evidence of the participant physically moving through a spatial environment as part of the described episode.

A2.1 Uncodified visual/auditory processing — the ramp's report of a 'tail-heavy' jacks reading is relayed verbally to the participant, not directly perceived by them, so this is better classified as information receipt (A2.4) rather than the participant's own perceptual interpretation.
A2.2 Literacy — while manifests, NOTOC, and logs are read, no substantive composition or interpretation of prose text is demonstrated beyond routine document use captured under A2.4.
A3.1, A3.2, A3.3, A3.5 — no serving, teaching, selling, or caring interactions described in this episode.
ambiguities: A2.1 vs A2.4 for the ramp's tail-heavy report: the participant does not personally observe the jacks reading, so this was classified as evaluated retrieved information (A2.4) rather than uncodified perceptual processing (A2.1); a different annotator could argue A2.1 applies transitively through the load-control profession.

evidence.quote: I signed and released with the figures as they stood. I weighed the delay risk—losing the slot—against a one-bag discrepancy...
evidence.explanation: The participant independently weighs competing operational risks and makes a final sign-off decision without describing a requirement to escalate for approval.

evidence.quote: so I shifted some of the cargo distribution forward before finalizing, beyond what my own computed index actually called for.
evidence.explanation: The participant exercises discretion to deviate from the computed index based on personal judgment.

evidence.quote: making sure the NOTOC is accurate before the captain gets it.
evidence.explanation: The captain reviews the NOTOC downstream, indicating some oversight, but no supervisor, audit, or real-time monitoring of the participant's decisions is described during the episode itself.

evidence.quote: About twenty minutes later, after the ramp had loaded per that instruction, they called up and said the aircraft was sitting slightly tail-heavy on the jacks reading.
evidence.explanation: The participant depends on ramp personnel for loading execution and for feedback that informs subsequent decisions, indicating functional collaboration though not sustained joint work.

evidence.quote: This particular one was a standard 45-minute turnaround, nothing scheduled to be unusual about it.
evidence.explanation: The participant frames the base task (building load sheets, issuing instructions, checking weight and balance) as routine and recurring, though this specific episode included several non-routine elements.

evidence.quote: There is one, for exactly this kind of non-standard cargo. I know it exists.
evidence.explanation: Existence of a formal manual limits chart and an automated ALI system indicates prescribed procedures and tools govern the work, even when not always followed.

evidence.quote: an LMC came in—roughly 380 kilos of mail plus six late bags that hadn't made the original manifest.
evidence.explanation: Base parameters (weights, structural limits) are well defined, but late changes and unexpected readings introduce meaningful uncertainty into an otherwise structured task.

evidence.quote: About that time, an LMC came in... they called up and said the aircraft was sitting slightly tail-heavy... the ramp tally was one bag short of what the NOTOC and manifest showed.
evidence.explanation: The episode is defined by a sequence of unplanned developments (irregular cargo, tail-heavy reading, late load change, tally discrepancy) each requiring an in-the-moment response.

tools.role_in_task: Generates the automatic load instruction (ALI) and supports trim/index calculations specific to weight-and-balance operations.

evidence.quote: Our load-control software generates an automatic load instruction—the ALI—and it put that machinery item into hold 3.
evidence.explanation: This is purpose-built software for load control, distinct from ordinary office ICT, meeting the specialised ICT definition.

evidence.quote: A couple of extra minutes with the trim computer, honestly. It wasn't unavailable.
evidence.explanation: The trim computer is a dedicated computational tool for weight-and-balance index calculations.

tools.role_in_task: Retrieval of dispatch log records to cross-check prior flight trim history.

evidence.quote: I pulled up the dispatch log because I wanted a sanity check before signing off.
evidence.explanation: Accessing a log/record system is consistent with routine digital record retrieval, though it could also be part of the specialised system; classified separately due to its general record-keeping function.

task_anchors.task_description: Accepting/issuing the automatically generated load instruction for an irregular cargo item without an independent manual check.
Evaluating a last-minute cargo change (LMC) by comparing its total weight against historical LMC patterns rather than running a placement-specific calculation.
Reviewing dispatch log history and adjusting cargo distribution based on an inferred rotation-level trend, beyond the flight's own computed index.
Weighing a one-bag manifest discrepancy against slot-timing risk before final sign-off and release.

I looked at the total weight and it was basically in line with the LMCs we'd been getting all week on this route.

missing_evidence: No direct evidence of the participant's own physical or perceptual involvement with cargo (e.g., visually inspecting the machinery item), limiting A1 and A2.1 classification.
No evidence of formal supervisory review or audit of the participant's decisions within the episode, limiting confidence in control_monitoring.
